beats.narration_text: Listing-cards has two parts. A scope selector that chooses your bundle — main, product-images, aplus, or full-set — and a CLI router that passes your short product description to the Higgsfield backend enhancer. The backend writes the actual generation prompts, runs the nano-banana-2 jobs, and returns the result URLs. Claude touches neither the prompts nor the images.

beats.narration_text: Law one: backend owns the prompts. Claude never writes the final image generation prompts for marketplace listings. As the SKILL says: do not write final image-generation prompts yourself. Backend enhancement owns that. The backend applies private compliance rules and templates that would be wrong to guess. You give it a short product description. It handles the rest.

props.heading: Backend owns the prompts.

beats.narration_text: Law two: scope first. The dash-dash scope flag selects a pre-built bundle: main for one image, product-images for six, aplus for eight, full-set for thirteen. You should never assemble individual assets manually when a scope covers your need. The SKILL says: use dash-dash scope when the user asks for a common bundle. Custom subsets with repeated dash-dash asset are for genuine edge cases only.

props.heading: Scope first.
props.body: main=1 image | product-images=6 | aplus=8 | full-set=13. Pick a scope before reaching for individual --asset flags.
props.quote: Use --scope when the user asks for a common bundle
props.sparkLine: One flag, a whole bundle. Don't assemble what scope gives you.

beats.narration_text: Law three: minimal interaction. As the SKILL says: ask at most one concise confirmation question before running. This isn't about being fast — it's about not blocking on questions when the product details are already clear. Prefer a product image. If text or a URL is the only input, proceed only when the product details are unambiguous.
